cognate: Gk ἑκυρή/ἑκυρός = SCr. svekrva/svekar = Ved. śvaśrū́/śváśura (*sweḱrúh₂/*swéḱuros); in the surrounding lines also δαήρ = dever = devṛ́ (*deh₂iwḗr), γάλως = zaova (*ǵl̥h₂ōws), εἰνάτερες = jetrve (*h₁yenh₂ter-)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic replaces the 'husband's sister' term with nánāndar; the rest of the set is kept
shared_syntax: a coordinated list of the husband's kin, mother-in-law and father-in-law paired (ἑκυρή ἑκυρός / svekar i svekrva), each set beside the bride; father-in-law likened to a father (πατὴρ ὣς / svekra k’o svoga babajka, Russ. svekra zvat' batjuškom)
context: the wife's standing in the husband's household seen from the bride's side: Helen's lament on how the δαέρες, γαλόῳ, εἰνάτερες and ἑκυρή treated her while Priam was gentle as a father; Serbian wedding/bridal songs listing deveri, zaove, jetrve, svekrva, svekar as kind or harsh (Vuk 36196:16-17 'evil mother-in-law, worse father-in-law'; 32932:6 'you will find svekar and svekrva'; 22086:144-147 'sisters-in-law as sisters ... father-in-law as own father'); RV 10.85.46 bride blessed to be queen over the same set
phrase: list of the husband's kin (*deh₂iwḗr, *ǵl̥h₂ōws, *h₁yenh₂ter-, *sweḱrúh₂, *swéḱuros) as the bride's new household, with the father-in-law 'as a father'
note: The kin terms themselves are inherited; what is shared is the bridal topos of enumerating the whole husband-side set together in one passage. Kin terms naturally co-occur, so the claim rests on the list being the same five-term set in the same bride's-eye frame across Greek, Serbian (and Vedic/Russian in support); the 'like a father' simile is natural and only corroborative. Serbian is a late tradition.

words: Ја сам била ... Више б'јела града

cognate: SCr. mjesec = Latv. mēness = Lith. mėnuo (*mḗh₁n̥s, masculine moon); SCr. zvijezda = Latv. zvaigzne (Balto-Slavic 'star')
drift_or_renewal: the morning star's name is renewed on each side: SCr. Danica (from 'day') ~ Latv. Auseklis / Lith. Aušrinė (from 'dawn', *h₂ews-)
shared_syntax: the masculine Moon as subject checking on the (feminine) morning star: SCr. Мјесец кара звијезду даницу 'the Moon scolds the morning star' + 'where have you been?' ~ Latv. Mēnesnīca zvaigznes skaita ... Auseklīša vien nebij 'the Moon counts the stars ... only Auseklis was missing'
context: mythological celestial-family songs: the Moon notes the morning star's absence and her whereabouts are told (Danica: over Belgrade watching the brothers divide their inheritance; Auseklis: in the sea in white foam); in Lithuanian (Nesselmann) the Moon's affair with Aušrinė is the subject of a reproachful question
phrase: Moon (*mḗh₁n̥s) and morning star: the Moon checks/reproaches the morning star for her absence
note: Shared at Balto-Slavic level only, with names renewed; Serbian uses the dialogue as an epic prologue, so this may be an inherited Balto-Slavic celestial motif or a regional folklore one; Vuk and dainos are late traditions.

ἔστ’ ἂν ὁ ἥλιος τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν ἴῃ

search_lead.cognate: SCr. sunce = Ved. sū́rya- = Gk ἥλιος (*sóh₂wl̥); SCr. nebo 'sky' renews Ved. diví (locative of dyú-)
search_lead.argument: Eternity/never-formula 'as long as the sun is in the sky / goes its course': Vuk 1658:315-316 'as long as (mounts) Cer and Vidojevica and sun and moon in the sky' ~ AVŚ 6.75.6 banishment 'for endless years, as long as the sun shall be in the sky' and AVP 19.9.19 'as long as heaven, as long as earth, as long as the sun shines' (earth-features + sun, as in Serbian); Hdt 8.143 Athenian oath 'as long as the sun goes the same road ... never'. Serbian 'teče' (the sun's running) matches Hdt's ὁδὸν ἴῃ in sense. Caveat: the formula is also Near Eastern (e.g. Ps. 72:5), so it may be typological.

drift_or_renewal: the preposition is renewed (kroz vs per); otherwise none
shared_syntax: verb of riding + prepositional phrase 'through the green forest', noun + adjective (гору зелену / žalią girę)
context: a rider on his horse going through the forest, the scene-opening formula of a song in both (Marko rides through the green forest and meets ...; Lith. 'when I rode through the green forest, my horse trembled')
